Weighted Seshadri constants
and ellipsoid embeddings

Jonny Evans
Abstract

We explore Seshadri constants associated to weighted blow-ups of complex projective varieties and demonstrate how to use this notion to construct symplectic embeddings of ellipsoids. We illustrate the utility of this point of view by providing constructions of full fillings of ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} by ellipsoids corresponding to all of the exceptional (post-Fibonacci) steps of the McDuff–Schlenk staircase and some non-obvious embeddings of ellipsoids in ellipsoids.

1 Introduction

1.1 Seshadri constants and symplectic geometry

Recall that:

  • •

    the Gromov width of a symplectic manifold (Z,ω)(Z,\omega) is the quantity π​r2\pi r^{2} where rr is the supremum over all radii of symplectically embedded balls in (Z,ω)(Z,\omega);

  • •

    the Seshadri constant of a projective variety ZZ at a point pp with respect to an ample divisor DD is defined to be the supremum sup{ε:g∗D−εC is ample}\sup\{\varepsilon\,:\,g^{*}D-\varepsilon C\text{ is ample}\}, where g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z is the blow-up of ZZ at pp and C=exc⁡(g)C=\operatorname{exc}(g) is the exceptional divisor.

It has been known since the work of McDuff and Polterovich [22] that there is a close connection between the Gromov width of a Kähler manifold and its Seshadri constants: the Seshadri constant gives a lower bound on the Gromov width (see Lazarsfeld’s book [18, Theorem 5.1.22]). One can generalise this to the problem of embedding several symplectic balls pairwise disjointly, which relates to the multi-point Seshadri constant. Biran [3, 4] proved that one can fully fill any symplectic 4-manifold with balls of equal size provided one has enough balls. In his ECM survey [5], Biran pointed out that one should be able to use weighted blow-ups instead of ordinary blow-ups and thereby study symplectic embeddings of ellipsoids.

Definition 1.1.1.

Given a vector 𝝈\bm{\sigma} of positive real numbers, the symplectic ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(𝝈)\mathbb{E}(\bm{\sigma}) is

𝔼⁡(𝝈)={𝒛∈ℂn:∑j=1n|zj|2σj≤1}⊂ℂn\mathbb{E}(\bm{\sigma})=\left\{\bm{z}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}\,:\,\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{|z_{j}|^{2}}{\sigma_{j}}\leq 1\right\}\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} (1.1)

where ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} is equipped with the standard symplectic form ∑k=1nd​xk∧d​yk\sum_{k=1}^{n}dx_{k}\wedge dy_{k} and zk=xk+i​ykz_{k}=x_{k}+iy_{k}. In the case when n=2n=2, we will refer to σ1/σ2\sigma_{1}/\sigma_{2} as the slope of the ellipsoid. If 𝔼⁡(𝝈)\mathbb{E}(\bm{\sigma}) embeds symplectically into a symplectic 4-manifold (Z,ω)(Z,\omega) then we refer to the ratio vol⁡(𝔼⁡(𝝈))/vol⁡(Z)\mathrm{vol}(\mathbb{E}(\bm{\sigma}))/\mathrm{vol}(Z) as the packing ratio.

The connection between weighted blow-up and ellipsoid embeddings was explored by McDuff [21]; McDuff showed that the problem of embedding a symplectic ellipsoid is equivalent to an associated ball packing problem. Similarly to Biran’s results, it follows that any symplectic 4-manifold admits a full filling by any symplectic ellipsoid of sufficiently large slope. For example, ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} can be fully filled by any ellipsoid of slope at least 28936\frac{289}{36} (see [23, Corollary 1.2.4]). The complete answer of which ellipsoids embed symplectically into ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} was worked out by McDuff and Schlenk in their seminal paper [23]. The size of the biggest ellipsoid embedding into ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} depends strongly on the slope of the ellipsoid: the set of possible pairs (a,b)∈ℝ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} for which there exists an embedding of 𝔼⁡(a,b)\mathbb{E}(a,b) forms a staircase-like shape. This staircase has infinitely many piecewise-linear steps; there is an infinite sequence of steps whose coordinates are related to the Fibonacci numbers, and which accumulate when the slope approaches the fourth power of the Golden Ratio. There are also nine “exceptional steps” beyond this slope. For slopes outside these steps, ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} can be fully filled (i.e. the packing ratio can be made arbitrarily close to 11).

Whilst much of the subsequent work on ellipsoid embeddings has used McDuff’s equivalence with ball-packings as a basis, the idea of working directly with weighted blow-ups has been used to great effect by Entov and Verbitsky [12] to show that full ellipsoid packings exist for Campana simple manifolds (Kähler manifolds which are not unions of their proper subvarieties). In the current paper, we adopt this point of view and show that it can also be used to find all of the ellipsoid embeddings in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} corresponding to the post-Fibonacci steps in the McDuff–Schlenk staircase.

1.2 Inflation

Biran’s main tool for constructing multiple balls and McDuff’s main tool for constructing ellipsoids is symplectic inflation, where one modifies a symplectic form along some curve in a 4-manifold; see for example [21, Proof of Proposition 2.1, Step 2]. Inflation along unicuspidal and sesquicuspidal plane curves is used by McDuff and Siegel in [24, Theorem A, E] to construct the full ellipsoid embeddings in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} corresponding to the Fibonacci portion of the staircase. Opshtein [27] showed that ellipsoids with slope p/qp/q could be constructed by inflating along a curve with “multi-cusp” singularities (points where several irreducible branches each modelled analytically on yp=xqy^{p}=x^{q}). In each case, one needs to pay careful attention to the local model for the inflationary curve.

Already in his ECM survey [5, Section 2.1], Biran pointed out that inflation is a symplectic analogue of using the Nakai–Moishezon criterion to find an ample divisor. In the current paper, we bypass inflation and just use Nakai–Moishezon, giving a purely algebro-geometric construction of symplectic ellipsoid embeddings.

1.3 Construction of ellipsoids

To a weighted blow-up g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z (see Definition 3.2.5) and an ample divisor DD on ZZ, we will associate a weighted Seshadri constant ε⁡(Z,D,g)\varepsilon(Z,D;g) (see Definition 3.1.2: this is the reciprocal of the Cutkosky–Ein–Lazarsfeld ss-invariant [9, Definition 1.1] of a certain ideal). One can use a lower bound on the weighted Seshadri constant to produce ellipsoids of a certain size. This is made precise in Theorem 1.3.1 below; essentially the same result appears in the paper of Entov and Verbitsky [12] with a complete and detailed proof in the masters thesis of Gudiev [15]. It was also proved in a different way by Luef and Wang [20, Theorem A], who also give an equivalent definition of weighted Seshadri constants in terms of plurisubharmonic functions with specified local behaviour [20, Definition 1.5 and Theorem 3.2]. We include a slightly different11 1 The idea in all the proofs is to produce Kähler forms which interpolate between standard forms on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} and its weighted blow-up. We use Guillemin–Abreu theory to reduce this to interpolation between convex functions on the moment polytope; both Entov–Verbitsky/Gudiev and Luef–Wang use Demailly’s regularised maximum of plurisubharmonic functions. proof here for completeness.

Theorem 1.3.1.

Let ZZ be a smooth complex projective variety, p∈Zp\in Z be a point and D⊂ZD\subset Z be an irreducible ample ℚ\mathbb{Q}-divisor; let ζ\zeta be the associated symplectic form Poincaré-dual to π​D\pi D (see Remark 2.1.4). Let g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z be a weighted blow-up with weight vector 𝐚=(a1,…,an)\bm{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}). Then (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) admits a symplectic embedding of the ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(εa1,…,εan)\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{a_{1}},\ldots,\frac{\varepsilon}{a_{n}}\right) for any rational ε<ε⁡(Z,D,g)\varepsilon<\varepsilon(Z,D;g).

To apply the theorem, you need a suitable divisor DD, which can be hard to find; this plays the role of the inflationary curve. We will illustrate the use of this theorem by constructing all of the exceptional steps in the McDuff–Schlenk staircase and constructing some new ellipsoid embeddings into ellipsoids. See Section 7 for a wide array of applications.

1.4 Advantages

There are several advantages to working in the category of complex projective varieties. First, the weighted blow-up is almost always singular, and the intersection theory of curves on singular projective varieties is well-developed and convenient to use. One could further resolve and work with a smooth manifold, but this ends up clouding the simplicity of computations with additional irrelevant terms. Second, one doesn’t need to make any assumptions on what the inflationary divisors look like, or how they intersect the exceptional divisor of the weighted blow-up: one simply applies the Nakai–Moishezon criterion to find an ample divisor and hence a symplectic form. Finally, we observe that the original construction of the exceptional steps by McDuff and Schlenk was quite involved: they had to enumerate all possible obstructive curves and find the strongest obstructions in each given interval of slopes. By contrast, as soon as we find a curve DD to which we can apply our construction, we find an ellipsoid.

1.5 Disadvantages and difficulties

There are also several disadvantages. The main disadvantage is that the method is wholly unsuitable for constructing ellipsoids whose slopes lie outside the steps of the McDuff–Schlenk staircase, that is when there is a one-parameter family of slopes which yield full fillings. To construct something arbitrarily close to the volume constraint one would need to use a certain infinite sequence of divisors DD and weighted blow-ups adapted to them, so that the associated weighted Seshadri constant gets closer and closer to a limiting value but never quite achieves it; see Example 7.4.2. It seems likely that this infinite sequence of divisors is precisely what one needs to prove the Nagata conjecture.

When working with weighted blow-ups there are also subtleties: there is not a single operation which, given a point and a slope, produces a canonical weighted blow-up. Indeed, one can construct weighted blow-ups by iteratedly blowing up at infinitely-near points and then contracting all but the last exceptional curve; the choices of which points one blows up give moduli for the construction; we explore this subtlety in Section 6.2. Rather than being a difficulty, this is really an advantage: we can make a “general” choice of points to blow-up, which can be helpful for constructing the right divisor DD.

1.6 Remarks on the proof of Theorem 1.3.1

Theorem 1.3.1 depends on some intermediate results (Proposition 5.7.1 and Corollary 5.7.2) which are weighted analogues of a result of McDuff and Polterovich’s [22, Corollary 2.1.D] for ordinary blow-ups. The strategy of our proof is very similar, but there are subtleties in modifying the proof to handle weighted blow-ups and ellipsoids:

  • 1.

    The McDuff–Polterovich proof uses Kähler forms constructed by pulling back the standard Kähler form on (ℂ×)n(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n} via a map of the form 𝒛↦h⁡(|𝒛|)|𝒛|​𝒛\bm{z}\mapsto\frac{h(|\bm{z}|)}{|\bm{z}|}\bm{z} for some strictly increasing function hh. These maps are called monotone embeddings. If one uses ∑j=1naj​|zj|2\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}|z_{j}|^{2}} instead of |𝒛||\bm{z}| then the pulled back form is not Kähler (it has (2,0)(2,0) and (0,2)(0,2)-parts), and it would be harder to check tameness. On a related note, the Hamiltonian circle action generated by H⁡(𝒛)=12​∑j=1naj​|zj|2H(\bm{z})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}|z_{j}|^{2} extends to a holomorphic ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}-action with weights a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n}, but this does not carry level sets of HH (ellipsoids) to level sets of HH unless 𝒂=(1,…,1)\bm{a}=(1,\ldots,1).

  • 2.

    The weighted blow-up of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} sits inside ℂn×ℙ⁡(𝒂)\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\mathbb{P}(\bm{a}) where ℙ⁡(𝒂)\mathbb{P}(\bm{a}) is a weighted projective space. The “standard” symplectic form on the ordinary blow-up can be written as a linear combination of two contributions: the pullback of the Fubini–Study form from the projection to ℙ⁡(1,…,1)\mathbb{P}(1,\ldots,1), and the pullback of the standard symplectic form on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. However, the symplectic form on the weighted blow-up cannot be written in this form: the inclusion of the weighted blow-up into the product has vanishing derivatives along the exceptional locus, so the pullback of the standard symplectic form has degeneracies along the normal directions to the exceptional locus of the weighted blow-up. Note that this is in addition to the complication that the weighted blow-up is singular.

To get around both of these issues, we use the Guillemin–Abreu theory of toric Kähler metrics and symplectic potentials on orbifolds to find “standard” symplectic forms and to interpolate between standard forms on the weighted blow-up and weighted blow-down.

1.7 Examples

In Section 7.1, we use the nodal cubic curve in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} as our divisor to construct embeddings of 𝔼⁡(σ1,σ2)\mathbb{E}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}) into ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} with:

  • •

    slope s≔σ2/σ1∈(7+452,7]s\coloneqq\sigma_{2}/\sigma_{1}\in\left(\frac{7+\sqrt{45}}{2},7\right] and packing ratios up to 9​s(1+s)2\frac{9s}{(1+s)^{2}}, and

  • •

    slope s≔σ2/σ1∈(7,649]s\coloneqq\sigma_{2}/\sigma_{1}\in\left(7,\frac{64}{9}\right] and packing ratios up to 64​s9\frac{64s}{9}.

These represent the optimal ellipsoid embeddings for the first post-Fibonacci step in the McDuff–Schlenk staircase. In Section 7.2, we use more complicated curves of higher degree to construct the remaining post-Fibonacci steps; these curves appear in the work of Dumnicki, Harbourne, Küronya, Roé and Szemberg [11] as “supraminimal curves”. In that context these curves are responsible for steps in a different but related staircase: the graph of the function μ^\hat{\mu} which is another way of getting at what we are calling the weighted Seshadri constant. Indeed, this paper grew out of my attempts to understand the relationship between their work and that of McDuff–Schlenk [23].

In Section 7.3, we explain how to reproduce the results of McDuff and Siegel [24] on ellipsoid embeddings via inflation along unicuspidal curves in our language, which in particular recovers the Fibonacci part of the staircase. In Sectino 7.4, we discuss the difficulties of using our method to produce embeddings when the staircase is not piecewise-linear. Finally, in Section 7.5, we give some examples of ellipsoid embeddings in other ellipsoids.

1.8 Outline

After recapping some prerequisites and fixing conventions (Section 2), we define what we mean by weighted blow-up and the associated Seshadri constants (Section 3). Then there follow two sections in which we explain how to iron out a Kähler form along the exceptional locus of a weighted blow-up (Section 4) and how to extend an ironed form over the blow-down (Section 5). Subsection 5.7 contains the proof of Theorem 1.3.1. Section 6 works out in detail how to calculate the weighted Seshadri constant in the case of complex surfaces and Section 7 applies this to a range of examples.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Notation, normalisations and conventions

Remark 2.1.1 (Broadcasting).

Throughout this paper, we will write expressions like 𝝁−1\bm{\mu}^{-1}, log⁡(𝝁)\log(\bm{\mu}), or ∂G∂𝝁\frac{\partial G}{\partial\bm{\mu}} where 𝝁=(μ1,…,μn)\bm{\mu}=(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n}) is a vector to mean the vector obtained by applying the relevant operation elementwise to 𝝁\bm{\mu} to obtain a new vector like (μ1−1,…,μn−1)(\mu_{1}^{-1},\ldots,\mu_{n}^{-1}), (log⁡(μ1),…,log⁡(μn))(\log(\mu_{1}),\ldots,\log(\mu_{n})), or (∂G/∂μ1,…,∂G/∂μn)(\partial G/\partial\mu_{1},\ldots,\partial G/\partial\mu_{n}). This practice, known as broadcasting, will simplify notation.

Remark 2.1.2 (Moment maps).

The standard moment map ℂn→ℝn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} sends 𝒛\bm{z} to

(12​|z1|2,…,12​|zn|2).\left(\frac{1}{2}|z_{1}|^{2},\ldots,\frac{1}{2}|z_{n}|^{2}\right).

The moment image of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} is the positive orthant, ℝ≥0n\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}. The moment image of the ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(𝝈)\mathbb{E}(\bm{\sigma}) is the subset

{𝝁∈ℝ≥0n:∑j=1nσi−1​μi≤12}\left\{\bm{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}\,:\,\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{-1}\mu_{i}\leq\frac{1}{2}\right\}

This has a slanted face with outward-pointing normal 𝝈−1=(σ1−1,…,σn−1)\bm{\sigma}^{-1}=(\sigma_{1}^{-1},\ldots,\sigma_{n}^{-1}). In this paper, we will assume that a positive multiple of this normal, say R​𝝈−1R\bm{\sigma}^{-1}, is a primitive integer vector 𝒂\bm{a}:

𝝈−1=R−1​𝒂.\bm{\sigma}^{-1}=R^{-1}\bm{a}.

It will often be more convenient to work with this normal, in which case we will write 𝔼⁡(R​𝒂−1)\mathbb{E}(R\bm{a}^{-1}). In terms of RR and 𝒂\bm{a}, the moment image of 𝔼⁡(R​𝒂−1)\mathbb{E}(R\bm{a}^{-1}) and its slanted face are:

Δ𝒂,R≔{𝝁∈ℝ≥0n:𝒂⋅𝝁≤R2},Λ𝒂,R≔{𝝁∈ℝ≥0n:𝒂⋅𝝁=R2}\Delta_{\bm{a},\,R}\coloneqq\left\{\bm{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}\,:\,\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\mu}\leq\frac{R}{2}\right\},\qquad\Lambda_{\bm{a},\,R}\coloneqq\left\{\bm{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}\,:\,\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\mu}=\frac{R}{2}\right\}
Remark 2.1.3 (Symplectic area and affine length).

Recall that the preimage of an edge of a moment polytope under a moment map is a symplectic sphere of symplectic area 2​π​ℓ2\pi\ell where ℓ\ell is the affine length of the edge. We will normalise the Fubini–Study form on ℂ​ℙn\mathbb{CP}^{n} as the symplectic reduction of the unit sphere in ℂn+1\mathbb{C}^{n+1}, so that it gives a line area π\pi: with this normalisation, the moment image is Λ(1,…,1), 1⊆ℝn+1\Lambda_{(1,\ldots,1),\,1}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, a nn-simplex whose edges have affine length 1/21/2.

Remark 2.1.4 (Symplectic forms from ample divisors).

Recall that if ZZ is a complex projective variety and DD is an ample ℚ\mathbb{Q}-Cartier ℚ\mathbb{Q}-divisor on ZZ then we obtain a Kähler form on the smooth locus of ZZ as follows. Let N>0N>0 be an integer such that N​DND is a very ample Cartier divisor and let LL be the associated line bundle. Since LL is very ample, evaluation of sections defines an embedding of ZZ into ℙ⁡(H0​(L)∨)\mathbb{P}(H^{0}(L)^{\vee}). Pulling back the Fubini–Study form along this embedding and then rescaling it by 1/N1/N yields a Kähler form whose cohomology class is Poincaré-dual to π​D\pi D.

Remark 2.1.5 (Orbifold Kodaira embedding).

We refer the reader to the lucid account of Ross and Thomas [31] for a helpful user’s guide to orbifolds. If ZZ is an orbifold then one can ask whether a Kähler form on the smooth locus extends to a Kähler orbifold differential form over the orbifold locus. Recall that an orbifold differential form is the same thing as a coherent choice of Γ\Gamma-invariant differential form on each local uniformising chart ℂn→ℂn/Γ\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}/\Gamma. Note that the Kähler form constructed in Remark 2.1.4 is degenerate along the orbifold locus when pulled back along a local uniformising chart ℂn→ℂn/Γ\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}/\Gamma. One can fix this by working instead with an orbi-ample orbibundle LL [31, Section 2.4 and Definition 2.7]. An orbibundle is locally just an equivariant line bundle on each orbifold chart; in particular, the stabiliser subgroup at a point z∈Zz\in Z acts on the line LzL_{z}. If we define the order ord⁡(Z)\mathrm{ord}(Z) to be the least common multiple of the sizes of point-stabilisers then L⊗ord⁡(Z)L^{\otimes\mathrm{ord}(Z)} is an honest line bundle. Ross and Thomas define an orbibundle to be locally ample if this action is faithful for all z∈Zz\in Z, and orbi-ample if it is locally ample and L⊗ord⁡(Z)L^{\otimes\mathrm{ord}(Z)} is ample. Given an orbi-ample line bundle, one can construct an orbifold embedding Z→ℙ⁡(𝒏)Z\to\mathbb{P}(\bm{n}) into a weighted projective space ℙ⁡(𝒏)\mathbb{P}(\bm{n}) built out of sections of powers of LL (see [31, Proposition 2.11]) and the pullback of the Fubini–Study orbifold Kähler form [31, Definition 3.3] yields an orbifold Kähler form on ZZ.

Background 2.1.6 (Intersection numbers).

We will frequently work with intersection numbers between divisors on singular complex projective surfaces; see [18, 1.1.C] for an explanation of how to make sense of this. If f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y is a morphism of schemes then we write f∗​Bf^{*}B for the total transform of a divisor B⊂YB\subset Y and f∗−1​Bf^{-1}_{*}B for its proper transform. We will make use of the push-pull formula: if f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y is a proper morphism of surfaces and A⊂XA\subset X and B⊂YB\subset Y are curves then

f∗​(A⋅f∗​B)=f∗​A⋅B.f_{*}(A\cdot f^{*}B)=f_{*}A\cdot B. (2.1)

See [32, Lemma 82.19.4, Tag 0EQT] for a more general statement at the level of Chow groups. For example, this tells us that:

  • •

    f∗−1​B⋅f∗​B=B2f^{-1}_{*}B\cdot f^{*}B=B^{2} since f∗​f∗−1​B=Bf_{*}f^{-1}_{*}B=B;

  • •

    if AA is contracted by ff then A⋅f∗​B=0A\cdot f^{*}B=0 since f∗​A=0f_{*}A=0.

3 Weighted Seshadri constants

3.1 Seshadri constants

Setup 3.1.1.

Let YY and ZZ be normal complex projective varieties and let g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z be a projective birational morphism with exceptional locus C=exc⁡(g)C=\operatorname{exc}(g). Let DD be an ample ℚ\mathbb{Q}-divisor on ZZ. Note that, by [17, Chapter II, Theorem 7.17], gg is the blow-up of ZZ along a coherent ideal sheaf ℐ\mathcal{I}.

Definition 3.1.2.

In the context of Setup 3.1.1, let Υε≔g∗​D−ε​C\Upsilon_{\varepsilon}\coloneqq g^{*}D-\varepsilon C and define the Seshadri constant of (Z,D)(Z,D) along gg to be

ε⁡(Z,D,g)≔sup{ε≥0:Υε​ is ample}.\varepsilon(Z,D;g)\coloneqq\sup\left\{\varepsilon\geq 0\,:\,\Upsilon_{\varepsilon}\text{ is ample}\right\}.

This Seshadri constant is precisely the reciprocal of the Cutkosky–Ein–Lazarsfeld ss-invariant of ℐ\mathcal{I}, see [9, Definition 1.1].

Remark 3.1.3.

Recall that a divisor Υ\Upsilon is called nef if Υ⋅A≥0\Upsilon\cdot A\geq 0 for all irreducible curves AA. One can equivalently define

ε⁡(Z,D,g)≔max⁡{ε≥0:Υε​ is nef}.\varepsilon(Z,D;g)\coloneqq\max\left\{\varepsilon\geq 0\,:\,\Upsilon_{\varepsilon}\text{ is nef}\right\}.

To see that this is equivalent to the definition using ampleness observe that g∗​D−ε​Cg^{*}D-\varepsilon C is ample for sufficiently small ε\varepsilon by [17, Chapter II, Proposition 7.10(b)]). By Kleiman’s theorem [18, Theorem 1.4.23] the nef cone of a projective scheme is the closure of its ample cone, so the path ε↦g∗​D−ε​C\varepsilon\mapsto g^{*}D-\varepsilon C leaves the ample cone at the last instant it is nef.

3.2 Weighted blow-ups

In this paper, we will focus on a specific class of ideal sheaves defining non-reduced points; we will call the corresponding blow-ups weighted blow-ups.

Definition 3.2.1.

Consider the cone σ\sigma spanned by the standard basis vectors 𝒆1,…,𝒆n\bm{e}_{1},\ldots,\bm{e}_{n}. The associated affine toric variety is 𝒵=ℂn\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{C}^{n}. Fix a primitive integer vector 𝒂∈ℤn\bm{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} with positive entries. Let ρ\rho be the ray pointing in the 𝒂\bm{a}-direction, and, for each j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, let σj\sigma_{j} be the cone spanned by 𝒂\bm{a} and all the basis vectors 𝒆k\bm{e}_{k} except 𝒆j\bm{e}_{j}. The cones σ1,…,σn\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n} now form a fan Σ𝒴\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}} subdividing σ\sigma. See Figure 1 for illustrations when n=2,3n=2,3.

Remark 3.2.2.

The fan Σ𝒴\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}} is the inward normal fan to the polytope

P𝒴​(R)≔{𝝁∈ℝ≥0n:𝒂⋅𝝁≥R/2}P_{\mathcal{Y}}(R)\coloneqq\{\bm{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}\,:\,\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\mu}\geq R/2\}

for any R>0R>0. This polytope is obtained from the positive orthant ℝ≥0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq 0} by chopping off a corner to obtain a new face Λ𝒂,R\Lambda_{\bm{a},\,R} with inward normal 𝒂\bm{a}. See Figure 1 for illustrations when n=2,3n=2,3.

Definition 3.2.3.

Let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be the normal toric variety associated to Σ𝒴\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}} and let g:𝒴→𝒵{g}\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z} be the toric morphism coming from the inclusion of the cones σj⊆σ\sigma_{j}\subseteq\sigma. The variety 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is a complex orbifold, with singularities at the toric fixed points, and the exceptional locus of g{g} is the toric divisor 𝒞\mathcal{C} associated to the ray ρ\rho. We call g{g} the toric weighted blow-up with weights 𝐚\bm{a}.

A weighted blow-up will be a blow-up locally analytically modelled on g:𝒴→𝒵{g}\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z}. To make this precise, let us define a family of subsets of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y}; at this point, these subsets could equally be balls or polydiscs rather than ellipsoids, but it will be more convenient to use ellipsoids later when we come to equip our varieties with Kähler forms.

Definition 3.2.4.

Given 𝒂\bm{a}, define the function H:𝒵→ℝH\colon\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R} by H⁡(𝒛)=∑j=1naj​|zj|2H(\bm{z})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}|z_{j}|^{2} whose level sets H−1​(R)H^{-1}(R) are the ellipsoids 𝒵⁡(R)≔𝔼⁡(R​𝒂−1)\mathcal{Z}(R)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}(R\bm{a}^{-1}). Let 𝒴⁡(R)=q−1​(𝒵⁡(R))\mathcal{Y}(R)=q^{-1}(\mathcal{Z}(R)).

Let ZZ be a smooth complex projective variety and p∈Zp\in Z be a point. Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be an ideal sheaf supported at pp and let g:Y=Blℐ​(Z)→Zg\colon Y=\mathrm{Bl}_{\mathcal{I}}(Z)\to Z be the corresponding blow-up. We say that gg is a weighted blow-up with weights 𝒂\bm{a} if there exists a commutative diagram of analytic morphisms

Remark 3.2.6.

Weighted blow-ups are more subtle than the ordinary blow-up, which is the special case 𝒂=(1,…,1)\bm{a}=(1,\ldots,1). For example:

  • •

    the ordinary blow-up depends on the holomorphic embedding ι\iota only through the value ι⁡(0)\iota(0), whereas more general weighted blow-ups depend heavily on this choice.

  • •

    the result of weighted blow-up with any weights other than (1,…,1)(1,\ldots,1) is always singular.

Using Cox’s homogeneous coordinate ring description of the toric variety associated to the fan Σ\Sigma, we see that 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is the GIT quotient of ℂn+1\mathbb{C}^{n+1} (with coordinates z0,z1,…,znz_{0},z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) by the ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}-action with weights −1,a1,…,an-1,a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}, that is t∈ℂ×t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} acts as

The unstable locus is z1=⋯=zn=0z_{1}=\cdots=z_{n}=0, so

g([z0:z1:⋯:zn])=(z0a1z1,…,z0anzn){g}([z_{0}:z_{1}:\cdots:z_{n}])=(z_{0}^{a_{1}}z_{1},\ldots,z_{0}^{a_{n}}z_{n})

The morphism (g,p):𝒴→𝒵×ℙ⁡(𝒂)({g},{p})\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z}\times\mathbb{P}(\bm{a}) is an injection whose image is the subscheme

{(z1,…,zn,[w1:⋯:wn]):zjakwkaj=zkajwjak for 1≤j,k≤n}.\left\{(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n},[w_{1}\,:\,\cdots\,:\,w_{n}])\,:\,z_{j}^{a_{k}}w_{k}^{a_{j}}=z_{k}^{a_{j}}w_{j}^{a_{k}}\text{ for }1\leq j,k\leq n\right\}.

The divisor (∏j=1naj)​𝒞\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}a_{j}\right)\mathcal{C} is Cartier. If Ti​jT_{ij} is the toric curve corresponding to the wall τi​j\tau_{ij} separating the top-dimensional cones σi\sigma_{i} and σj\sigma_{j} then,

Remark 3.2.9.

Note that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is actually “orbi-Cartier” in the sense that it is the vanishing set of a section of an orbifold line bundle. Namely, let ℒ\mathcal{L} be the quotient of ℂ×(ℂn∖0)×ℂ\mathbb{C}\times\left(\mathbb{C}^{n}\setminus 0\right)\times\mathbb{C} by ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times} acting with weights (−1,a1,…,an,−1)(-1,a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},-1); this has an orbibundle projection ℒ→𝒴\mathcal{L}\to\mathcal{Y} and [z0:z1:⋯:zn]↦[z0:z1:⋯:zn:z0][z_{0}:z_{1}:\cdots:z_{n}]\mapsto[z_{0}:z_{1}:\cdots:z_{n}:z_{0}] defines a section which vanishes precisely along 𝒞\mathcal{C}. This line bundle is locally ample in the sense of Remark 2.1.5. If g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z is a weighted blow-up with exc⁡(g)=C\operatorname{exc}(g)=C and N⁡(g∗​D−ε​C)N(g^{*}D-\varepsilon C) is an ample Cartier divisor then, as remarked in Remark 2.1.5, the resulting Kähler form will be degenerate at the orbifold points. In other words, we can assume that Υε\Upsilon_{\varepsilon} is orbi-ample in the definition of the Seshadri constant, and that we are working with genuine orbifold Kähler forms.

4 Ironing

Given a Kähler manifold, McDuff and Polterovich have a procedure for “ironing” a symplectic form to make it flat near a point whilst keeping it tame (see [22, Lemma 5.5.B]). To blow down, we need to be able to iron our symplectic forms to make them “standard” along the exceptional locus. We need some lemmas, whose proofs closely follow those of McDuff and Polterovich.

For convenience, let us order our basis of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} so that the entries of the vector 𝒂\bm{a} satisfy

a1≤a2≤⋯≤an.a_{1}\leq a_{2}\leq\cdots\leq a_{n}.

We will continue to write g:𝒴→𝒵{g}\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z} for the toric weighted blow-up of 𝒵=ℂn\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{C}^{n} with weights 𝒂\bm{a}, and we also write ω𝒵\omega_{\mathcal{Z}} for the standard symplectic form on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}.

    κ2​ω𝒵\kappa^{2}\omega_{\mathcal{Z}} on the ball of radius εκ​R3​an\frac{\varepsilon}{\kappa}\sqrt{\frac{R}{3a_{n}}}, which contains the ellipsoid 𝒵⁡(R​ε2​a14​κ2​an)\mathcal{Z}\left(\frac{R\varepsilon^{2}a_{1}}{4\kappa^{2}a_{n}}\right).∎

5 Kähler forms

5.1 Review of Guillemin–Abreu theory

We will make extensive use of the Guillemin–Abreu theory of toric Kähler geometry. We briefly recap what we need from this theory; the reader can learn more from the original paper by Guillemin [16] or the subsequent work by Abreu [1, 2] which also treats the orbifold setting. Recall that a Kähler structure on a manifold XX comprises a complex structure JJ and a symplectic form ω\omega which are compatible in the sense that, at every point pp,

ω⁡(J​v,J​w)=ω⁡(v,w)\omega(Jv,Jw)=\omega(v,w)

for all tangent vectors v,w∈Tp​Xv,w\in T_{p}X and ω⁡(v,J​v)>0\omega(v,Jv)>0 for all nonzero tangent vectors vv (this second condition is called tameness: ω\omega tames JJ). If XX is an orbifold locally modelled on a quotient ℂn/Γ\mathbb{C}^{n}/\Gamma by the action of a finite group Γ⊂G​L​(n,ℂ)\Gamma\subset GL(n,\mathbb{C}) then we can still talk about Kähler structures: they just come from Γ\Gamma-invariant Kähler structures on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}.

Let ℓ1,…,ℓm:ℝn→ℝ\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m}\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} be linear maps and R1,…,RmR_{1},\ldots,R_{m} be real numbers. The linear inequalities ℓi​(𝝁)≥Ri/2\ell_{i}(\bm{\mu})\geq R_{i}/2 cut out a polytope

P={𝝁∈ℝn:ℓi(𝝁)≥Ri/2 for i=1,…,m}.P=\left\{\bm{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\,:\,\ell_{i}(\bm{\mu})\geq R_{i}/2\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\right\}.

Given this polytope, we can construct:

  • •

    the normal toric variety 𝒳\mathcal{X} (a complex orbifold) associated with the inward normal fan to PP. This admits a holomorphic (ℂ×)n(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n}-action which has a free Zariski-open orbit. We identify this Zariski-open torus with ℂn/(2​π​ℤ)n\mathbb{C}^{n}/(2\pi\mathbb{Z})^{n} via the exponential map, writing complex coordinates 𝝀+i​𝜽\bm{\lambda}+i\bm{\theta} with 𝝀=(λ1,…,λn)∈ℝn\bm{\lambda}=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and 𝜽=(θ1,…,θn)∈ℝn/(2​π​ℤ)n\bm{\theta}=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}/(2\pi\mathbb{Z})^{n}, so that the action of 𝒕=(t1,…,tn)∈Tn⊆(ℂ×)n\bm{t}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n})\in T^{n}\subseteq(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n} is given by 𝝀+i⁡(𝜽+𝒕)\bm{\lambda}+i(\bm{\theta}+\bm{t}). We refer to these as complex coordinates. The notation 𝝀\bm{\lambda} is intended to evoke “log-radius”.

  • •

    a toric symplectic orbifold (𝔛,ω)(\mathfrak{X},\omega) together with a moment map 𝝁:𝔛→P\bm{\mu}\colon\mathfrak{X}\to P. This construction is due to Lerman and Tolman [19], following Delzant’s construction in the case of manifolds [10]. This admits a Hamiltonian action of the torus TnT^{n} which is free over the interior P∘⊆PP^{\circ}\subseteq P of the moment polytope. The 𝝁\bm{\mu}-preimage of P∘P^{\circ} is symplectomorphic to P∘×TnP^{\circ}\times T^{n} equipped with the symplectic form ω=∑j=1nd​μi∧d​θi\omega=\sum_{j=1}^{n}d\mu_{i}\wedge d\theta_{i} where (μ1,…,μn)(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n}) are linear coordinates on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and (θ1,…,θn)∈Tn=ℝn/(2​π​ℤ)n(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n})\in T^{n}=\mathbb{R}^{n}/(2\pi\mathbb{Z})^{n} are angle coordinates such that the circle action generated by μj\mu_{j} rotates θj\theta_{j} at unit speed. We refer to these as symplectic (or action-angle) coordinates.

The orbifolds 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝔛\mathfrak{X} are diffeomorphic, and the Guillemin–Abreu theory tells us how to combine the symplectic and complex geometry to obtain a (torus-invariant) Kähler structure on either side. There are many torus-invariant Kähler structures, and choosing one is equivalent to choosing a symplectic potential:

Definition 5.1.1 (Symplectic potential).

A symplectic potential is a strictly convex function G:P→ℝG\colon P\to\mathbb{R} of the form

G⁡(𝝁)=∑i=1mL⁡(ℓi​(𝝁)−Ri/2)+h⁡(𝝁)G(\bm{\mu})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}L(\ell_{i}(\bm{\mu})-R_{i}/2)+h(\bm{\mu})

where:

  • •

    L⁡(t)=12​(t​log⁡(2​t)−t)L(t)=\frac{1}{2}(t\log(2t)-t).

  • •

    h⁡(𝝁)h(\bm{\mu}) is a smooth function on PP.

  • •

    (detHess⁡(G))⋅∏i=1m(ℓi​(𝝁)−Ri/2)\left(\det\operatorname{Hess}(G)\right)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}(\ell_{i}(\bm{\mu})-R_{i}/2) is strictly positive along ∂P\partial P.

Remark 5.1.2.

Guillemin and Abreu use the function 12​t​log⁡t\frac{1}{2}t\log t instead of our LL. These functions differ only by a linear term, which can be absorbed into hh. This is also responsible for the factor of 1/21/2 in Ri/2R_{i}/2 which will pervade our equations. The advantage of our choice is that it yields the standard symplectic form and moment map on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}.

Construction 5.1.3.

We use a symplectic potential to define a torus-invariant complex structure on 𝔛\mathfrak{X} compatible with ω\omega. In terms of the symplectic coordinates (𝝁,𝜽)(\bm{\mu},\bm{\theta}) on the open set 𝝁−1​(P∘)\bm{\mu}^{-1}(P^{\circ}), the complex structure is given by the block matrix

J=(0−Hess​(G)−1Hess⁡(G)0).J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\mathrm{Hess}(G)^{-1}\\ \mathrm{Hess}(G)&0\end{pmatrix}.

Integrability of JJ is equivalent to the fact that the off-diagonal blocks are Hessian matrices for some function GG. Abreu [2, Appendix A] explains why this complex structure extends over the toric boundary. The complex orbifold (𝔛,J)(\mathfrak{X},J) is biholomorphic to (𝒳,i)(\mathcal{X},i) via an explicit biholomorphism Ψ:𝔛→𝒳\Psi\colon\mathfrak{X}\to\mathcal{X}. In symplectic and complex coordinates, Ψ\Psi can be written as:

Ψ⁡(𝝁+i​𝜽)=ψ⁡(𝝁)+i​𝜽,ψ⁡(𝝁)=∂G∂𝝁.\Psi(\bm{\mu}+i\bm{\theta})=\psi(\bm{\mu})+i\bm{\theta},\qquad\psi(\bm{\mu})=\frac{\partial G}{\partial\bm{\mu}}.

Moreover, the pullback (Ψ−1)∗​ω(\Psi^{-1})^{*}\omega on 𝝁−1​(P∘)⊆𝒳\bm{\mu}^{-1}(P^{\circ})\subseteq\mathcal{X} can be written as 2​i​∂∂¯​F2i\partial\bar{\partial}F for a Kähler potential

F⁡(𝝀+i​𝜽)=𝝀⋅ψ−1​(𝝀)−G⁡(ψ−1​(𝝀))F(\bm{\lambda}+i\bm{\theta})=\bm{\lambda}\cdot\psi^{-1}(\bm{\lambda})-G(\psi^{-1}(\bm{\lambda}))

In other words, FF is the Legendre transform of GG and λj\lambda_{j} is the conjugate variable to μj\mu_{j}. The moment map for the torus action is given by projection to 𝝁\bm{\mu} in symplectic coordinates and by ψ−1​(𝝀)=∂F∂𝝀\psi^{-1}(\bm{\lambda})=\frac{\partial F}{\partial\bm{\lambda}} in complex coordinates; that is, the moment map is given by the conjugate variables to 𝝀\bm{\lambda}.

Remark 5.1.4.

Changing the symplectic potential by a linear term doesn’t affect the Hessian; it does affect the Kähler potential and the moment map.

which fill out the whole of m𝒂,R∂\textcjheb{m}_{\bm{a},\,R_{\partial}}; see Figure 4. I highlight this because the main difference between complex and symplectic (weighted) blow-up is that in the symplectic case one usually thinks of “cutting out a ball” whereas in the complex case one “cuts out a point”. This example shows how to equip the ball punctured at a point with a symplectic form in such a way that it appears that a whole ball has been excised.

5.4 Implanting a weighted blow-up

For the purposes of performing the weighted blow-up, we need a symplectic form on 𝒴\mathcal{Y} which coincides with the flat Kähler form g∗​ω𝒵{g}^{*}\omega_{\mathcal{Z}} outside 𝒴⁡(R)\mathcal{Y}(R) for sufficiently large RR. In fact, we will only need the construction in the other direction (blowing down), but we explain weighted blowing up for completeness.

Given a complex manifold ZZ and a weighted blow up

with weights 𝐚\bm{a}, suppose that ZZ admits a tame symplectic form ω\omega such that ι∗​ω=ω𝒵\iota^{*}\omega=\omega_{\mathcal{Z}}. The symplectic form ω𝒴ironed\omega^{\operatorname{ironed}}_{\mathcal{Y}} coincides with ω𝒴R0,𝟎\omega^{R_{0},\bm{0}}_{\mathcal{Y}} in a neighbourhood of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and so makes CC symplectomorphic to the toric orbifold with moment image Λ𝒂,R0\Lambda_{\bm{a},\,R_{0}}. ∎

Remark 5.4.4.

By [22, Lemma 5.5.B], if we have an almost Kähler manifold (Z,ω,J)(Z,\omega,J) and a holomorphic embedding ι:𝒵⁡(R)→Z\iota\colon\mathcal{Z}(R)\to Z for some RR, we can “iron” the symplectic form near to ι⁡(0)\iota(0) to get a new symplectic form ω′\omega^{\prime} taming JJ such that ι∗​ω′\iota^{*}\omega^{\prime} coincides with a multiple of ω𝒵\omega_{\mathcal{Z}} on some 𝒵⁡(R′)⊆𝒵⁡(R)\mathcal{Z}(R^{\prime})\subseteq\mathcal{Z}(R) and ω′\omega^{\prime} coincides with ω\omega on the complement of ι⁡(𝒵⁡(R))\iota(\mathcal{Z}(R)). Therefore we can always perform the weighted blow-up along a sufficiently small ellipsoid after ironing.

5.7 Proof of Theorem 1.3.1

We begin with some preliminary results.

Proposition 5.7.1.

Given a complex manifold ZZ and a weighted blow up

with weights 𝐚\bm{a}, suppose that YY admits a symplectic form υ\upsilon such that:

Then there exists a symplectic structure ω\omega on ZZ such that:

  • (1)

    ω\omega tames the complex structure,

    g∗​ω=υg^{*}\omega=\upsilon on the complement of ȷ⁡(𝒴⁡(R∂))\jmath(\mathcal{Y}(R_{\partial})),

Choose a 0<R0<R∂0<R_{0}<R_{\partial} and let r1r_{1} be such that r1​R0=Rr_{1}R_{0}=R. Then r1​ω𝒴⁡(R∂)R0r_{1}\omega^{R_{0}}_{\mathcal{Y}(R_{\partial})} is a Kähler form on 𝒴⁡(R∂)\mathcal{Y}(R_{\partial}) whose pullback to 𝒞=exc⁡(g)\mathcal{C}=\operatorname{exc}({g}) is cohomologous to that of ȷ∗​υ\jmath^{*}\upsilon. Now we appeal to Lemma 4.2.1 and iron υ\upsilon on ȷ⁡(𝒴⁡(R∂))\jmath(\mathcal{Y}(R_{\partial})) to get a new taming form υ′\upsilon^{\prime} such that:

  • •

    the pullback ȷ∗​υ′\jmath^{*}\upsilon^{\prime} has the property that, for some SS and r2r_{2}, its restriction to 𝒴⁡(S)\mathcal{Y}(S) coincides with r1​ω𝒴⁡(R∂)R0+r2​g∗​ω𝒵r_{1}\omega^{R_{0}}_{\mathcal{Y}(R_{\partial})}+r_{2}{g}^{*}\omega_{\mathcal{Z}}.

By Proposition 5.6.1, this contains a copy of 𝔼⁡(r1​R0​𝒂−1)=𝔼⁡(R​𝒂−1)\mathbb{E}(r_{1}R_{0}\bm{a}^{-1})=\mathbb{E}(R\bm{a}^{-1}) as required. ∎

Corollary 5.7.2.

Let ZZ be a smooth complex projective variety of dimension nn equipped with a Kähler form ζ\zeta, and let g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z be a weighted blow-up with weights 𝐚\bm{a} and exceptional locus exc⁡(g)=C⊆Y\operatorname{exc}(g)=C\subseteq Y. Suppose that YY admits a Kähler form υ\upsilon such that:

  • •

    the pullback of υ\upsilon to C=exc⁡(g)C=\operatorname{exc}(g) is cohomologous to the toric symplectic form coming from the moment polytope Λ𝒂,R\Lambda_{\bm{a},\,R} for some RR, and

  • •

    the restrictions of υ\upsilon and g∗​ζg^{*}\zeta to Y∖CY\setminus C are cohomologous.

Then (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) admits a symplectic embedding of the ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(R​𝐚−1)\mathbb{E}(R\bm{a}^{-1}).

Proof.

By Proposition 5.7.1, ZZ admits a symplectic form ω\omega taming the complex structure such that (Z,ω)(Z,\omega) contains a copy of the desired ellipsoid. But since ζ\zeta and ω\omega both tame the same complex structure, the 2-forms t​ω+(1−t)​ζt\omega+(1-t)\zeta are all symplectic. Their restrictions to the complement of the ellipsoid where the blow-up is happening are cohomologous by assumption, and the ellipsoid is contractible, so they are cohomologous on ZZ. We can then apply Moser’s trick to this path of symplectic forms; we see that they are symplectomorphic. Therefore (Z,ω)(Z,\omega) also contains a copy of 𝔼⁡(R​𝒂−1)\mathbb{E}(R\bm{a}^{-1}). ∎

We finally explain how Theorem 1.3.1 follows from Corollary 5.7.2.

If we take R=ε​∏k=1nakR=\varepsilon\prod_{k=1}^{n}a_{k} and consider the toric symplectic form υtoric\upsilon_{\operatorname{toric}} on the local model of the toric weighted blow-up, then we get

6 Weighted Seshadri constants for surfaces

We now focus on the case of complex surfaces. We will free up some subscripts by switching from writing 𝒂=(a1,a2)\bm{a}=(a_{1},a_{2}) to writing 𝒂=(α,β)\bm{a}=(\alpha,\beta) for the weights of a weighted blow-up.

6.1 Local model

Let g:𝒴→𝒵{g}\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z} be the toric weighted blow-up of 𝒵=ℂ2\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{C}^{2} at the origin with weights (α,β)(\alpha,\beta). This is associated to the fan Σ\Sigma with three rays:

ℝ≥0​(α,β),ℝ≥0​(0,1),ℝ≥0​(1,0).\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(\alpha,\beta),\qquad\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(0,1),\qquad\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(1,0).

The fan Σ\Sigma is the inward normal fan to the polygon (see Figure 10):

P𝒴​(R0)={(μ1,μ2)∈ℝ≥02:α​μ1+β​μ2≥R0/2}.P_{\mathcal{Y}}(R_{0})=\{(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{\geq 0}\,:\,\alpha\mu_{1}+\beta\mu_{2}\geq R_{0}/2\}.

where [a,b,c,…]=a−1b−1c−⋯.\displaystyle\text{where }[a,b,c,\ldots]=a-\frac{1}{b-\frac{1}{c-\cdots}}.

Note that the proper transform f∗−1​𝒞{f}^{-1}_{*}\mathcal{C} is ℰi1\mathcal{E}_{i_{1}} and (αi1,βi1)=(α,β)(\alpha_{i_{1}},\beta_{i_{1}})=(\alpha,\beta). The curves E1,…,Ei1−1E_{1},\ldots,E_{i_{1}-1} (respectively Ei1+1,…,EmE_{i_{1}+1},\ldots,E_{m}) project to the point labelled 𝔭\mathfrak{p} (respectively 𝔮\mathfrak{q}) in Figure 10.

Remark 6.1.1.

As usual, we will use script/nonscript letters to denote the local/non-local versions of this, so if g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z is a weighted blow-up and f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y is its minimal resolution then we will write E1,…,EmE_{1},\ldots,E_{m} and CC for the exceptional curves of h≔g∘fh\coloneqq g\circ f and gg respectively, and Ei1=f∗−1​CE_{i_{1}}=f^{-1}_{*}C.

Remark 6.1.2.

Note that since f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y is a minimal resolution, we have Ei2≤−2E_{i}^{2}\leq-2 for all i≠i1i\neq i_{1}. Since ZZ is smooth at pp, h=g∘fh=g\circ f is not a minimal resolution (there’s nothing to resolve) which means that Ei12=−1E_{i_{1}}^{2}=-1.

6.2 The Farey tree

Even if ZZ is toric and pp is a toric fixed point, not all weighted blow-ups at pp are globally toric: there is a lot of freedom in forming weighted blow-ups, and, in this section, we will discuss the moduli space of weighted blow-ups at pp.

Discussion 6.2.1.

Since Ei1E_{i_{1}} is a −1-1-curve (Remark 6.1.2), we may contract it. Then one of the neighbouring curves Ei2E_{i_{2}} must become a −1-1-curve. Contracting Ei2E_{i_{2}} and continuing in this manner, we contract all the remaining curves in some order Ei3,…,EimE_{i_{3}},\ldots,E_{i_{m}} until we get back to ZZ. Reversing this argument, we see that any weighted blow-up can be obtained by iteratedly blowing up at points infinitely near to pp: write F1=EimF_{1}=E_{i_{m}} for the first exceptional curve, then blow up a point on F1F_{1} with exceptional curve F2=Eim−1F_{2}=E_{i_{m-1}}, then blow up a point on F2F_{2} with exceptional curve F3=Eim−2F_{3}=E_{i_{m-2}}, and so on. Provided we end up with a linear chain of curves, we will call such a blow-up process a Farey process.

Ensuring the curves remain in a linear chain constrains which blow-ups we can perform. We call the intersection points between curves in the chain satellite points. If the most recent exceptional curve FiF_{i} has two satellite points pip_{i} and qiq_{i} then, in order that our exceptional set remains a linear chain, we can only blow up at a satellite point. If, however, FiF_{i} has only one satellite point then we can either blow up at this satellite point pip_{i} or else at any other (free) point qiq_{i} of FiF_{i}. Once we have blown up at a satellite point, we encounter no further free points, but there is always a choice between two satellite points. We think of this as a decision tree (see Figure 12).

Definition 6.2.2 (Farey tree).

If we label the nodes of this decision tree with the weights of the corresponding weighted blow-up, we obtain the well-known Farey tree of primitive integer vectors; see Figure 12. The easiest way to reconstruct these labels is to first label each node by three integer vectors 𝒖,𝒗,𝒘\bm{u},\bm{v},\bm{w}, starting with the root which is labelled (1,0),(1,1),(0,1)(1,0),(1,1),(0,1). Moving up from the node 𝒖,𝒗,𝒘\bm{u},\bm{v},\bm{w}, if we move rightward in the decision tree, the next node is labelled 𝒗,𝒗+𝒘,𝒘\bm{v},\bm{v}+\bm{w},\bm{w} and if we move leftward then the next node is labelled 𝒖,𝒖+𝒗,𝒗\bm{u},\bm{u}+\bm{v},\bm{v}. Then if a node is labelled 𝒖,𝒗,𝒘\bm{u},\bm{v},\bm{w}, we omit the 𝒖\bm{u} and 𝒘\bm{w} and just keep the label 𝒗\bm{v}. Here, we think of the first step as a rightward step, so the first node above the root is labelled (1,2)(1,2).

Remark 6.2.3.

We will always write our chains E1,…,EmE_{1},\ldots,E_{m} from left to right and think of satellite points being ordered with pip_{i} on the left and qiq_{i} on the right (so pi∈Ek−1∩Ekp_{i}\in E_{k-1}\cap E_{k} and qi∈Ek∩Ek+1q_{i}\in E_{k}\cap E_{k+1} for some kk).

Definition 6.2.4.

The choices of free points in a Farey process can be fixed ahead of time by picking the germ of an irreducible analytic curve AA passing through pp. At the first step, we blow up the intersection of F1F_{1} with the proper transform of AA. At the second step, we take q2q_{2} to be the unique intersection point A∩F2A\cap F_{2}. If we blow up at q2q_{2}, we can take q3q_{3} to be the unique intersection point A∩F3A\cap F_{3}, and so on. We call this the Farey process guided by AA.

Remark 6.2.5.

Given a Farey process, we can always choose the analytic curve germ44 4 This germ is purely local: it does not need to be part of a closed holomorphic curve in XX. AA at the end passing transversely through a non-satellite point of the right-most curve EmE_{m} in the chain. Contracting down to ZZ we obtain a smooth, irreducible curve germ whose guided Farey process coincides with the given process.

Example 6.2.6.
  • (1)

    The toric weighted blow-up is guided by (either) one of the toric boundary components passing through pp.

  • (2)

    Let Z=ℂ​ℙ2Z=\mathbb{CP}^{2}, let p=[0:0:1]p=[0:0:1], and take AA to be the nodal cubic curve {[x:y:z]:x3+y3=xyz}\{[x:y:z]\,:\,x^{3}+y^{3}=xyz\}. Under the Farey process of weight (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) guided by (either) one of the branches of AA, the proper transform of AA is always an embedded, irreducible rational curve which intersects E1E_{1} and EmE_{m} once transversely. This fails to be toric if β/α>2\beta/\alpha>2: if we move right once in the Farey tree then the point q2q_{2} where the proper transform of AA intersects F2F_{2} is not a toric fixed point, and the blow-up at q2q_{2} is not toric.

Lemma 6.2.7.

Suppose ZZ is a smooth complex projective surface and let g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z be a morphism of projective surfaces whose exceptional locus is an irreducible rational curve CC. Let f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y be the minimal resolution. If the exceptional locus of h=g∘fh=g\circ f is a chain of curves E1,…,EmE_{1},\ldots,E_{m} then gg is a weighted blow-up.

Proof.

We can contract −1-1-curves on XX one at a time starting with f∗−1​Cf^{-1}_{*}C until we get to ZZ, so XX is obtained from ZZ by a Farey process. Let AA be a smooth curve germ through pp guiding this Farey process as in Remark 6.2.5. Since AA is smooth, in suitable local analytic coordinates ι:𝒵⁡(R)→Z\iota\colon\mathcal{Z}(R)\to Z we can take it to be y=0y=0. But since this is the toric boundary in 𝒵⁡(R)\mathcal{Z}(R), this guides the toric blow-up of 𝒵⁡(R)\mathcal{Z}(R). ∎

Remark 6.2.8.

In fact, we do not need to assume that YY is projective: since XX is obtained by iterated blow-up from ZZ, we see that XX is projective. Now let DD be an ample divisor on ZZ. The divisor L=f∗​(g∗​D−ε​C)L=f^{*}(g^{*}D-\varepsilon C) satisfies L⋅Ej=0L\cdot E_{j}=0 for j≠i1j\neq i_{1} and L⋅Ei1=ε/(α​β)>0L\cdot E_{i_{1}}=\varepsilon/(\alpha\beta)>0, so for large NN, the linear system |N​L||NL| defines a morphism to ℙ⁡(|N​L|)\mathbb{P}(|NL|) which factors as X→fY→iℙ⁡(|N​L|)X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\to}}Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\to}}\mathbb{P}(|NL|) for some projective embedding ii of YY.

Remark 6.2.9.

If Z=ℂ​ℙ2Z=\mathbb{CP}^{2} and we are given an Zariski-open affine coordinate chart (not just analytic) then we can rotate so that the tangent space of any smooth guiding curve AA at p=[0:0:1]p=[0:0:1] is y=0y=0 so that the germ of AA is equivalent to the curve y=ξ⁡(x)y=\xi(x) for some analytic function ξ\xi.

Remark 6.2.10.

We will usually be more interested in “sufficiently general” Farey processes, where any free choice is made at a “sufficiently general” point of FiF_{i}. Recall that the divisor Fm⊆XF_{m}\subseteq X gives a divisorial valuation on the function field of ZZ, and there is a notion of “very general quasimonomial valuation” (see [11]), which means that the coefficients of the power series ξ⁡(x)\xi(x) from Remark 6.2.9 are chosen to lie in the complement of a countable union of algebraic sets. In practice, however, the following easily checkable condition will suffice.

Definition 6.2.11.

Consider an Farey process whose result is X→𝑓Y→𝑔ZX\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z and let h=g∘fh=g\circ f. Given a rational curve A⊆ZA\subseteq Z we write A≈=h∗−1​A\accentset{\approx}{A}=h^{-1}_{*}A for its proper transform. We say that this Farey process is general with respect to AA if A≈\accentset{\approx}{A} is an embedded rational curve with A≈2≥−1\accentset{\approx}{A}^{2}\geq-1. We say it is adapted to AA if it is general with respect to AA and A≈2=−1\accentset{\approx}{A}^{2}=-1.

Remark 6.2.12.

If we were to deform the arbitrary choices of blow-up points slightly then the homology class [A≈][\accentset{\approx}{A}] would still contain an embedded rational curve, so this condition is stable under small perturbations, hence “general”. Adaptedness is a condition that will be useful when we are trying to maximise the weighted Seshadri constant ε⁡(Z,A,g)\varepsilon(Z,A;g).

Example 6.2.13.

Let AA be a nodal cubic curve from Example 6.2.6(2). If we perform a Farey process guided by AA then the self-intersection of the curve A≈\accentset{\approx}{A} is equal to 6−r6-r where rr is the number of times we move right in the Farey tree before moving left. Equivalently, this Farey process is general with respect to AA provided β/α≤7\beta/\alpha\leq 7 and adapted to AA if 6<β/α≤76<\beta/\alpha\leq 7. By contrast, the toric Farey process is adapted to AA if and only if β/α≤2\beta/\alpha\leq 2.

The weighted Seshadri constant satisfies

Remark 6.3.5.

Note that Υε\Upsilon_{\varepsilon} is effective (i.e. a non-negative linear combination of curves) if and only if ε≤δ\varepsilon\leq\delta. If δ<D2C⋅D~\delta<\frac{D^{2}}{C\cdot\widetilde{D}} then μ⁡(Z,D,g)=δ\mu(Z,D;g)=\delta gives us a lower bound on the weighted Seshadri constant, but ε⁡(Z,D,g)\varepsilon(Z,D;g) could in principle be larger. This will usually mean that when we produce ellipsoids in the regime δ<D2C⋅D~\delta<\frac{D^{2}}{C\cdot\widetilde{D}}, they will not be optimal (they could possibly be made larger). In this case, we say we are in the ineffective regime.

Remark 6.3.6.

If D2C⋅D~≤δ\frac{D^{2}}{C\cdot\widetilde{D}}\leq\delta then Lemma 6.3.4 computes the weighted Seshadri constant: as ε\varepsilon approaches its maximal value, the “symplectic area” Υε⋅D~\Upsilon_{\varepsilon}\cdot\widetilde{D} goes to zero. Indeed, as we will see, this is precisely the symplectic area of D~\widetilde{D} for a symplectic form associated to the projective embedding coming from the linear system of a large multiple of Υε\Upsilon_{\varepsilon}. Now pass to the minimal resolution f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y and take the proper transform D≈=f∗−1​D~\accentset{\approx}{D}=f^{-1}_{*}\widetilde{D}. Suppose that (the reduced curve underlying55 5 We will usually take DD to be a rational multiple of a reduced curve, so this just means “drop the coefficient”.) D≈\accentset{\approx}{D} has non-zero Gromov–Witten invariant (for example, it could be an embedded rational curve of square −1-1). Since such a curve needs to have positive symplectic area, it will provide an obstruction to taking ε\varepsilon any larger. For this reason, if D2C⋅D~≤δ\frac{D^{2}}{C\cdot\widetilde{D}}\leq\delta, we say that we are in the potentially obstructive regime, and if moreover D≈\accentset{\approx}{D} has nonzero Gromov–Witten invariant, we say that we are in the obstructive regime.

Evidently, the number C⋅D~C\cdot\widetilde{D} is the most important thing to calculate in order to apply this lemma. This can be achieved using the following lemma.

Lemma 6.3.7.

C⋅D~=∑i=1mγi​Ei⋅D≈.C\cdot\widetilde{D}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\gamma_{i}E_{i}\cdot\accentset{\approx}{D}.

Now substituting in the values of γi\gamma_{i} from Equation (6.3) gives the result (recall that f∗−1​C=Ei1f^{-1}_{*}C=E_{i_{1}}, α=αi1\alpha=\alpha_{i_{1}} and β=βi1\beta=\beta_{i_{1}}). ∎

7 Examples

7.1 Nodal cubic

Let AA be the nodal cubic curve in the plane defined by the equation {xyz=x3+y3}⊆ℂℙ2\{xyz=x^{3}+y^{3}\}\subseteq\mathbb{CP}^{2}. We will make a weighted blow-up with weights (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) with slope β/α\beta/\alpha in the interval (6,8](6,8] which is adapted to AA in the sense of Definition 6.2.11. This will give us large values of the weighted Seshadri constant ε⁡(ℂ​ℙ2,13​A,g)\varepsilon(\mathbb{CP}^{2},\frac{1}{3}A;g) which will in turn enable us to embed large ellipsoids whose slopes lie within this interval. More precisely, we will prove the following:

Proposition 7.1.1.

Equip ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} with the Fubini–Study form which gives a line area 11.

  • (a)

    For all s∈(7+452,7]s\in\left(\frac{7+\sqrt{45}}{2},7\right] and for all σ1<3​s1+s\sigma_{1}<\frac{3s}{1+s} and σ2<31+s\sigma_{2}<\frac{3}{1+s}, the ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(σ1,σ2)\mathbb{E}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}) embeds symplectically in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2}.

  • (b)

    For all s∈[7,649]s\in\left[7,\frac{64}{9}\right] and for all σ1<8​s3\sigma_{1}<\frac{8s}{3} and σ2<83\sigma_{2}<\frac{8}{3}, the ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(σ1,σ2)\mathbb{E}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}) embeds symplectically in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2}.

Remark 7.1.2.

These are the optimal ellipsoid embeddings for the first exceptional step in the McDuff-Schlenk staircase [23]: one cannot embed larger ellipsoids with these slopes. Note that 7+452≈6.85410\frac{7+\sqrt{45}}{2}\approx 6.85410 is the fourth power of the Golden Ratio.

Proof.

(a) The nodal cubic AA has two irreducible branches at p=[0:0:1]p=[0:0:1]. Let f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y be the minimal resolution. Note that A≈=f∗−1​g∗−1​A\accentset{\approx}{A}=f^{-1}_{*}g^{-1}_{*}A intersects the left-most and right-most curves E1E_{1} and EmE_{m} in the chain each once transversely:

A≈⋅E1=A≈⋅Em=1,A≈⋅Ej=0 if j≠1,m.\accentset{\approx}{A}\cdot E_{1}=\accentset{\approx}{A}\cdot E_{m}=1,\qquad\accentset{\approx}{A}\cdot E_{j}=0\text{ if }j\neq 1,m.

μ⁡(ℂ​ℙ2,D,g)=min⁡(α​β​C⋅D~,D2C⋅D~)=min⁡(α+β3,3​α​βα+β)\displaystyle\mu(\mathbb{CP}^{2},D;g)=\min\left(\alpha\beta C\cdot\widetilde{D},\frac{D^{2}}{C\cdot\widetilde{D}}\right)=\min\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{3},\frac{3\alpha\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\right)

Remark 7.1.3.

The reason the packing ratios are optimal in both these cases is that we are in the obstructive regime (see Remark 6.3.6). In other words, the curve D≈\accentset{\approx}{D} is an embedded rational curve of square −1-1 in the minimal resolution, and so has non-zero Gromov–Witten invariant, and as we approach the weighted Seshadri constant its area goes to zero, so it provides an obstruction to making the ellipsoid bigger. If we lie in the interval (6,8](6,8] but outside either of the subintervals listed in Proposition 7.1.1 then we are in the ineffective regime. Whilst we are still able to construct ellipsoids from this, they usually fail to be optimal: there is no obstructive curve whose area goes to zero.

7.2 Steps beyond the Fibonacci staircase

The nodal cubic example enabled us to construct optimal embeddings for all ellipsoids in the range of slopes between 7+452\frac{7+\sqrt{45}}{2} and 649\frac{64}{9}. In fact, we can also construct optimal ellipsoids for all of the piecewise linear steps in the McDuff–Schlenk staircase beyond the Fibonacci range (we will refer to these as the exceptional steps). We will work out in detail the most complicated step, which has its midpoint at 7⁤2157\frac{2}{15}, and give enough information for the reader to be able to reconstruct the remaining steps following the same reasoning.

A similar analysis can be used with all the other curves in Figure 14 to find the remaining exceptional steps of the McDuff–Schlenk staircase. 7.3 Unicuspidal curves

McDuff and Siegel [24] use unicuspidal and sesquicuspidal curves to produce ellipsoids for the Fibonacci portion of the McDuff–Schlenk staircase. Recall that a (p,q)(p,q)-cusp is a singularity locally analytically modelled on the curve germ {(x,y)∈ℂ2:yp=xq}\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\,:\,y^{p}=x^{q}\}, where gcd⁡(p,q)=1\gcd(p,q)=1; a (p,q)(p,q)-unicuspidal curve is a curve with a unique singular point which is a (p,q)(p,q)-cusp, and a (p,q)(p,q)-sesquicuspidal curve is allowed to have some additional nodal singularities. Theorem A(a) of [24] explains how to use such a curve to produce symplectic ellipsoids. We illustrate how our methods work in this context by proving the following result:

Proposition 7.3.1.

Let A⊆ℂ​ℙ2A\subseteq\mathbb{CP}^{2} be an irreducible curve of degree dd with a (p,q)(p,q)-cusp (and possibly other singular points). Then:

  • •

    for any slope ss in the interval d2/q2<s<p/qd^{2}/q^{2}<s<p/q there is a symplectic embedding of 𝔼⁡(dq,dq​s)\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{d}{q},\frac{d}{qs}\right) into ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2},

  • •

    and for any slope ss in the interval p/q≤s<p2/d2p/q\leq s<p^{2}/d^{2} there is a symplectic embedding of 𝔼⁡(pd,pd​s)\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{p}{d},\frac{p}{ds}\right) into ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2}.

In particular, we get full fillings for slopes s=d2q2s=\frac{d^{2}}{q^{2}} and s=p2d2s=\frac{p^{2}}{d^{2}}.

Proof.

The (p,q)(p,q)-cusp admits a toric weighted blow-up with weights (q,p)(q,p) so that the proper transform of the cusp is a curve intersecting the final blow-up curve FmF_{m} once transversely. Since AA has a singular point modelled locally analytically on this cusp, we can perform the corresponding weighted blow-up on ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} (note that this need no longer be toric since the local analytic chart around the cusp will not be toric).

As usual, we will take D=A/dD=A/d. Given a slope s=β/αs=\beta/\alpha, we can perform a Farey process with weights (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) which follows the Farey process guided by the cusp as far as it can in the Farey tree. If s<p/qs<p/q (respectively s≥p/qs\geq p/q) then A≈\accentset{\approx}{A} will intersect the resolution chain E1,…,EmE_{1},\ldots,E_{m} somewhere to the right (respectively left) of Ei1E_{i_{1}} so we will have C⋅D~=qd​αC\cdot\widetilde{D}=\frac{q}{d\alpha} (respectively C⋅D~=pd​βC\cdot\widetilde{D}=\frac{p}{d\beta}). This gives

μ(ℂℙ2,D;g)=min(αβC⋅D~,1C⋅D~)={min⁡(β​qd,d​αq) if βα<pq,min⁡(p​αd,d​βp) if pq≤βα.\mu(\mathbb{CP}^{2},D;g)=\min\left(\alpha\beta C\cdot\widetilde{D},\frac{1}{C\cdot\widetilde{D}}\right)=\begin{cases}\min\left(\frac{\beta q}{d},\frac{d\alpha}{q}\right)&\text{ if }\frac{\beta}{\alpha}<\frac{p}{q},\\ \min\left(\frac{p\alpha}{d},\frac{d\beta}{p}\right)&\text{ if }\frac{p}{q}\leq\frac{\beta}{\alpha}.\end{cases}

Therefore if d2q2<s<pq\frac{d^{2}}{q^{2}}<s<\frac{p}{q} or pq≤s<p2d2\frac{p}{q}\leq s<\frac{p^{2}}{d^{2}} then we are in the potentially obstructive regime and, by Lemma 6.3.4,

ε(ℂℙ2,D;g)=μ(ℂℙ2,D;g)={d​αq if d2q2<s<pq,d​βp if ​pq≤s<p2d2.\varepsilon(\mathbb{CP}^{2},D;g)=\mu(\mathbb{CP}^{2},D;g)=\begin{cases}\frac{d\alpha}{q}&\text{ if }\frac{d^{2}}{q^{2}}<s<\frac{p}{q},\\ \frac{d\beta}{p}&\text{ if }\frac{p}{q}\leq s<\frac{p^{2}}{d^{2}}.\end{cases}

Now Theorem 1.3.1 gives the ellipsoids we seek. The packing ratios are d2q2​s\frac{d^{2}}{q^{2}s} if s<p/qs<p/q and p2d2​s\frac{p^{2}}{d^{2}s} if s>p/qs>p/q, so we get full fillings when s=d2/q2s=d^{2}/q^{2} or s=p2/d2s=p^{2}/d^{2}. ∎

Remark 7.3.2.

Note that outside the intervals mentioned in the statement of Proposition 7.3.1, we are in the ineffective regime and if we tried to construct ellipsoids with such slopes using the same curve AA, they would end up being suboptimal.

Example 7.3.3.

Let F1,F2,F3,F4,F5,…=1,1,2,3,5,…F_{1},F_{2},F_{3},F_{4},F_{5},\ldots=1,1,2,3,5,\ldots denote the Fibonacci sequence and recall that, for each k≥1k\geq 1, there is an (F2​k+1,F2​k+5)(F_{2k+1},F_{2k+5})-unicuspidal curve of degree F2​k+3F_{2k+3}; see [28, Theorem C(a)]. When applied to these curves, Proposition 7.3.1 yields the Fibonacci stairs. Indeed, in this case the proper transform of AA is an embedded rational −1-1-curve, so we are in the obstructive regime and the ellipsoids are optimal.

Example 7.3.4.

There is a (64,9)(64,9)-unicuspidal curve of degree 2424 and genus 11. This can be obtained from a smooth cubic (degree 33) by applying a suitable Orevkov twist (which is a birational automorphism of ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} of degree 88) – see for example [6, Example 8.18] or [7, Proof of Corollary 5.28]. In this case, d2/q2=p/q=p2/d2=64/9d^{2}/q^{2}=p/q=p^{2}/d^{2}=64/9, so we obtain ellipsoids 𝔼⁡(a,b)⊆ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{E}(a,b)\subseteq\mathbb{CP}^{2} for any a<8/3a<8/3 and any b<3/8b<3/8. This gives another construction of the full fillings with slope s=64/9s=64/9.

Remark 7.3.5.

If one can find a (p2,q2)(p^{2},q^{2})-unicuspidal curve of degree p​qpq in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} then one would obtain a full filling with slope p2/q2p^{2}/q^{2}; by the adjunction formula, such a curve would necessarily have positive genus. One might try to construct such a curve by applying a birational transformation of degree pp to a smooth curve of degree qq (Example 7.3.4 is the case p=8p=8, q=3q=3). As we saw, the exceptional steps of the McDuff–Schlenk staircase give us full fillings of ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} at the rational slopes s=1072402s=\frac{107^{2}}{40^{2}}, 432162\frac{43^{2}}{16^{2}}, 352132\frac{35^{2}}{13^{2}}, 22282\frac{22^{2}}{8^{2}} and 17262\frac{17^{2}}{6^{2}}. It would be nice to know if there exist corresponding unicuspidal curves.

Remark 7.3.6.

One could also allow more general cusps, with multiple Puiseux pairs. The overall effect of this would be to change the value of C⋅D~C\cdot\widetilde{D} by a multiplicative constant: the only difference is that unique branch of A≈\accentset{\approx}{A} would now hit the curve labelled (p,q)(p,q) in the Farey tree non-transversely, with some intersection number kk. The effect in the calculations is to replace pp and qq by k​pkp and k​qkq. Compare with [24, Theorem A(b)].

7.4 Full fillings outside the steps?

As remarked in Section 1.5, this method usually does not seem to produce optimal ellipsoids whose slopes lie in intervals where full fillings exist, in other words for any slope ss between 7+452\frac{7+\sqrt{45}}{2} and ∞\infty which does not lie on one of the nine McDuff–Schlenk steps. The exception is when the slope is a square number s=d2s=d^{2}. Such full fillings were constructed by Opshtein [26, Lemma 2.1]: the neighbourhood of a smooth curve of degree dd is a ball subbundle of its symplectic normal bundle, and the total space of the restriction of this bundle to an open ball in the smooth curve is an ellipsoid of slope d2d^{2}. McDuff gave an alternative construction of the same ellipsoid [21, Proposition 2.1] by inflating along the smooth curve of degree dd. To illustrate the connection with our method, we explain his result in our language before going on to show why things are harder for other slopes.

Proposition 7.4.1 (Opshtein [26]).

There is a symplectic embedding of 𝔼⁡(ε,ε/d2)\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/d^{2}) into ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} for any integer dd and any ε<d\varepsilon<d.

Proof.

Let AA be a smooth curve of degree dd passing through p=[0:0:1]p=[0:0:1]. Consider the Farey process guided by AA corresponding to the path in the Farey tree which simply moves right d2d^{2} times; this produces a weighted blow-up g:Y→ℂ​ℙ2g\colon Y\to\mathbb{CP}^{2} with weights (1,d2)(1,d^{2}) where the proper transform of AA intersects Ed2E_{d^{2}} once transversely. If we use D=A/dD=A/d then C⋅D~=1/dC\cdot\widetilde{D}=1/d and, by Lemma 6.3.4, the weighted Seshadri constant is ε(ℂℙ2,D;g)=μ(ℂℙ,D;g)=d\varepsilon(\mathbb{CP}^{2},D;g)=\mu(\mathbb{CP}^{,}D;g)=d, so Theorem 1.3.1 gives embeddings of 𝔼⁡(ε,ε/d2)\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/d^{2}) for all ε<d\varepsilon<d as required. ∎

Example 7.4.2.

Now let us focus on the slope s=10s=10. Let g:Y→Zg\colon Y\to Z be a weighted blow-up with weights (α,β)=(1,10)(\alpha,\beta)=(1,10) and let f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y be the minimal resolution: the exceptional locus of g∘fg\circ f is a chain of curves E1,…,E10E_{1},\ldots,E_{10} with self-intersections E12=⋯=E92=−2E_{1}^{2}=\cdots=E_{9}^{2}=-2 and E10=−1E_{10}=-1. Suppose we find a curve A⊆ℂ​ℙ2A\subseteq\mathbb{CP}^{2} whose proper transform A≈\accentset{\approx}{A} satisfies A≈⋅Ei=φi\accentset{\approx}{A}\cdot E_{i}=\varphi_{i}. Then C⋅A~=k10C\cdot\widetilde{A}=\frac{k}{10} where k=∑i=110i​φik=\sum_{i=1}^{10}i\varphi_{i}, so if we take D=A/dD=A/d then we get C⋅D~=k/(10​d)C\cdot\widetilde{D}=k/(10d) and

ε⁡(ℂ​ℙ2,D,g)=min⁡(10​C⋅D~,1/C⋅D~)=min⁡(k/d,10​d/k).\varepsilon(\mathbb{CP}^{2},D;g)=\min(10C\cdot\widetilde{D},1/C\cdot\widetilde{D})=\min(k/d,10d/k).

If k/d<10k/d<\sqrt{10} then the weighted Seshadri constant equals k/dk/d and we get an ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(k/d,k/(10​d))\mathbb{E}(k/d,k/(10d)) with packing ratio k2/(10​d2)k^{2}/(10d^{2}). If k/d≥10k/d\geq\sqrt{10} then the weighted Seshadri constant equals 10​d/k10d/k and we get an ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(10​d/k,d/k)\mathbb{E}(10d/k,d/k) with packing ratio 10​d2/k210d^{2}/k^{2}. Clearly we can never achieve a packing ratio of 11 because 10\sqrt{10} is irrational. However, we can try and get close if we are able to find a curve where k/dk/d is a good rational approximation to 10\sqrt{10}. The continued fraction expansion of 10\sqrt{10} and the first few convergents are:

10=3+16+16+⋯:196,11737,721228,⋯\sqrt{10}=3+\frac{1}{6+\frac{1}{6+\cdots}}:\qquad\frac{19}{6},\qquad\frac{117}{37},\qquad\frac{721}{228},\qquad\cdots

Let AA be a rational sextic curve with an A18A_{18} singularity and a node: such curves exist, see for example [33, p.223, Table 2 (cont.): first column, penultimate row] or [29, §1.2] for an explicit rational parametrisation. Blow-up the A18A_{18} singularity: the proper transform of AA has an A16A_{16} singularity on the exceptional curve. Continue blowing up the singular point of the proper transform until we have blown up nine times. The two branches of the germ of AA separate at this point and intersect E9E_{9} transversely. Blow up one of these two intersection points. The result is precisely a chain E1,…,E10E_{1},\ldots,E_{10} and

φi=A≈⋅Ei={1 if i=9,100 otherwise.\varphi_{i}=\accentset{\approx}{A}\cdot E_{i}=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if }i=9,10\\ 0&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

This gives k=19k=19 and d=6d=6, so we find ellipsoids 𝔼⁡(a,b)\mathbb{E}(a,b) for any a<10​d/k=60/19a<10d/k=60/19 and b<d/k=6/19b<d/k=6/19. Although we are in the potentially obstructive regime, the curve A≈\accentset{\approx}{A} is a nodal rational curve of square −1-1 which has negative virtual dimension and hence has vanishing Gromov–Witten invariant and does not provide an obstruction to enlarging the ellipsoid.

Remark 7.4.3.

It seems that to find optimal ellipsoids using this technique, one would need to find a whole sequence of curves AA of higher and higher degrees so that k/d→10k/d\to\sqrt{10}. This has the same flavour as finding a sequence of rays in the ample cone which converge to the Nagata ray.

7.5 Ellipsoids in ellipsoids

The final example we give is motivated by a question asked to us by Kyler Siegel, namely which ellipsoids pack into other ellipsoids? Let 2≤k<ℓ2\leq k<\ell be relatively prime positive integers. By making a symplectic cut along its boundary, one can compactify the ellipsoid 𝔼⁡(k,ℓ)\mathbb{E}(k,\ell) inside the weighted projective plane ℙ⁡(k,ℓ,1)\mathbb{P}(k,\ell,1); let [x:y:z][x:y:z] be weighted homogeneous coordinates on ℙ⁡(k,ℓ,1)\mathbb{P}(k,\ell,1) and T={z=0}T=\{z=0\} be the compactifying divisor, so that 𝔼⁡(k,ℓ)=ℙ⁡(k,ℓ,1)∖T\mathbb{E}(k,\ell)=\mathbb{P}(k,\ell,1)\setminus T. We will produce ellipsoid embeddings in ellipsoids by first embedding them into weighted projective planes and then observing that the resulting embedding can be disjoined from TT by an isotopy.

Theorem 7.5.1.

Let β,α\beta,\alpha be coprime positive integers with s=β/α>12​(k​ℓ−2+k2​ℓ2−4​k​ℓ)s=\beta/\alpha>\frac{1}{2}(k\ell-2+\sqrt{k^{2}\ell^{2}-4k\ell}). For any ε<k​ℓ​α​βα+β\varepsilon<\frac{k\ell\alpha\beta}{\alpha+\beta} there is a symplectic embedding 𝔼⁡(ε/β,ε/α)→𝔼⁡(k,ℓ)\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon/\beta,\varepsilon/\alpha)\to\mathbb{E}(k,\ell).

Proof.

Take weighted homogeneous coordinates [x:y:z][x:y:z] on Z≔ℙ⁡(k,ℓ,1)Z\coloneqq\mathbb{P}(k,\ell,1) and consider the curve D={xyzk​ℓ−k−ℓ=xℓ+yk}D=\{xyz^{k\ell-k-\ell}=x^{\ell}+y^{k}\} of weighted degree k​ℓk\ell. This is an ample Cartier divisor with D2=k​ℓD^{2}=k\ell (note that DD is numerically equivalent to k​ℓ​Tk\ell T and T2=1/(k​ℓ)T^{2}=1/(k\ell)). In the smooth affine chart z=1z=1, DD is locally analytically equivalent to x​y=0xy=0 (or x​y=y2xy=y^{2} if k=2k=2), so it has a nodal singularity. Taking a Farey process with weights (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) guided by a branch of DD we obtain a weighted blow-up g:Y→Z=ℙ⁡(k,ℓ,1)g\colon Y\to Z=\mathbb{P}(k,\ell,1) such that the proper transform D~\widetilde{D} intersects the left- and right-most curves E1E_{1} and EmE_{m} each once transversely, so C⋅D~=1β+1α=α+βα​βC\cdot\widetilde{D}=\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\alpha}=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}. We have

μ⁡(ℙ⁡(k,ℓ,1),D,g)=min⁡(α+β,k​ℓ​α​βα+β).\mu(\mathbb{P}(k,\ell,1),D;g)=\min\left(\alpha+\beta,\frac{k\ell\alpha\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\right).

We are in the potentially obstructive regime when k​ℓ​α​βα+β<α+β\frac{k\ell\alpha\beta}{\alpha+\beta}<\alpha+\beta, which is equivalent to

s≔β/α>12​(k​ℓ−2+k2​ℓ2−4​k​ℓ).s\coloneqq\beta/\alpha>\frac{1}{2}(k\ell-2+\sqrt{k^{2}\ell^{2}-4k\ell}).

In this case, the weighted Seshadri constant is

ε⁡(ℙ⁡(k,ℓ,1),D,g)=μ⁡(ℙ⁡(k,ℓ,1),D,g)=k​ℓ​α​βα+β=k​ℓ​s​α1+s\varepsilon(\mathbb{P}(k,\ell,1),D;g)=\mu(\mathbb{P}(k,\ell,1),D;g)=\frac{k\ell\alpha\beta}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac{k\ell s\alpha}{1+s}

so Theorem 1.3.1 should give us the ellipsoids we seek. However, there is a minor issue here: in Theorem 1.3.1, we assumed ZZ to be smooth, but now ZZ is only an orbifold, and DD is only ample (not orbi-ample). We can fix this by instead using the orbi-ample divisor N​D+TND+T for sufficiently large NN; this works because TT is locally ample. The only other place where smoothness of ZZ is needed is in the proof of Corollary 5.7.2, where we used Moser’s argument to show that (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) (the symplectic manifold we started with) is symplectomorphic to (Z,ω)(Z,\omega) (the symplectic manifold obtained by weighted blow-down). Provided we work with orbifold symplectic forms, nondegenerate along the orbifold locus, Moser’s argument works just as well for orbifolds: one simply constructs the orbifold diffeomorphism by working Γ\Gamma-invariantly in the local uniformising cover. Since the resulting Moser-diffeomorphisms preserve the orbifold locus, the ellipsoids we construct are disjoint from the orbifold locus.

The ellipsoids we produce in (Z,ω)(Z,\omega) are manifestly disjoint from TT, and the arguments of [22, Remark 2.1.E and Corollary 4.1.B] apply in the orbifold setting, using the symplectic tubular neighbourhood theorem for suborbifolds [25, Proposition 17], to show that we can modify the Moser isotopy to ensure that the ellipsoids in (Z,ζ)(Z,\zeta) remain in the complement of TT. Therefore we produce symplectic embeddings 𝔼⁡(α,β)→𝔼⁡(k,ℓ)\mathbb{E}(\alpha,\beta)\to\mathbb{E}(k,\ell). ∎

Remark 7.5.2.

As ε\varepsilon approaches the Seshadri constant, the packing ratio approaches s+s−1+2k​ℓ\frac{s+s^{-1}+2}{k\ell}. As s→12​(k​ℓ−2+k2​ℓ2−4​k​ℓ)s\to\frac{1}{2}(k\ell-2+\sqrt{k^{2}\ell^{2}-4k\ell}), this approaches 11, so we get fuller and fuller fillings. Note that the slopes of these fillings are substantially larger than ℓ/k\ell/k, the slope of 𝔼⁡(k,ℓ)\mathbb{E}(k,\ell).

Remark 7.5.3.

If we take k=1k=1 then the proof breaks down: the curve DD is no longer nodal. Instead, if ℓ>1\ell>1, one should look at A={xyzℓ−1=xℓ+y2}A=\{xyz^{\ell-1}=x^{\ell}+y^{2}\} of weighted degree 2​ℓ2\ell and take D=12​AD=\frac{1}{2}A. The conclusion is modified accordingly: for all slopes s>2​ℓ−1+4​ℓ2−ℓs>2\ell-1+4\sqrt{\ell^{2}-\ell} we get an embedding of 𝔼⁡(ε/β,ε/α)\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon/\beta,\varepsilon/\alpha) into 𝔼⁡(1,ℓ)\mathbb{E}(1,\ell) whenever ε<2​ℓ​α​βα+β\varepsilon<\frac{2\ell\alpha\beta}{\alpha+\beta}. If k=1k=1 and ℓ=1\ell=1 then we need to pass to cubics and we are back in the situation of Proposition 7.1.1.

Remark 7.5.4.

Clearly this is just one family of ellipsoid embeddings, analogous to the first post-Fibonacci step of the McDuff–Schlenk staircase explained in Proposition 7.1.1. The full story of ellipsoids in ellipsoids remains to be worked out.
